item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Kid-friendly Hikes Under 3 Miles

One Oakland redwood trail runs a flat, paved mile and a half that a stroller finishes, rated 4.7 stars by the people who actually walked it. Most East Bay parents keep circling the same three crowded parks. Eight East Bay kid hikes under three miles, each with the real mileage and climb.

Stream Trail to Trail's End — Canyon Meadow staging, 7867 Redwood Rd, Oakland, in Redwood Regional Park. 1.7 miles, 91 feet of gain, paved and stroller-friendly, 4.7 stars. The one even a four-year-old finishes. @ebrpd

Sequoia Bayview and Big Trees Loop — Joaquin Miller Park, 3540 Sanborn Dr, Oakland. 2 miles, 219 feet of gain, easy, 4.7 stars. A coast-redwood loop with a bay view.

Overlook and Round Top Loop — Sibley Volcanic Preserve, 6800 Skyline Blvd, Oakland. 1.7 miles, 246 feet of gain, 4.6 stars. A loop around the Bay Area's own extinct volcano.

Lower and Upper Huckleberry Loop — Huckleberry Botanic Preserve, Skyline Blvd, Oakland. 2.3 miles, 367 feet of gain, 4.7 stars. A rare-plant preserve big on birdsong, no dogs on this one.

East West and Upper Jordan Fire Trail — Claremont Canyon Regional Preserve, Claremont Ave, Berkeley. 2.2 miles, 620 feet of gain, 4.6 stars. A short climb that pays off with the full bay and bridge.

Grizzly Peak, Tower, and Golf Course Loop — Tilden Regional Park, Grizzly Peak Blvd, Berkeley. 2.6 miles, 442 feet of gain, 4.5 stars. Ridge views over the whole East Bay.

French, Tres Sendas, and Stream Loop — Canyon Meadow staging, 7867 Redwood Rd, Oakland, in Redwood Regional Park. 2.5 miles, 456 feet of gain, 4.8 stars. The highest-rated of the set, deep in the redwoods.

Sunset, Sequoia Bay View, and Chaparral Loop — Joaquin Miller Park, 3540 Sanborn Dr, Oakland. 2.8 miles, 416 feet of gain, 4.6 stars. Save it for a west-facing sunset finish.

Eight under three miles: the paved Stream Trail, Sequoia Bayview, Round Top, Huckleberry, Claremont Canyon, Grizzly Peak, the French loop, and the Sunset ridge. Which one gets the first Saturday?

item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Summit Hikes, Easy to Hard

The pole at the top of Mission Peak is the most photographed spot in the East Bay, and you earn it with 2,145 feet of climbing. But not every East Bay summit makes you suffer, one is a two mile volcano loop. Nine summit hikes, easy to hard, with the grade and route on each.

Mission Peak Loop — Stanford Ave staging, Fremont, in Mission Peak Regional Preserve. 6.1 miles, 2,145 feet of gain, hard, loop, 4.7 stars. The pole at the summit selfie hike. @ebrpd

Mount Diablo via Summit Trail — Mount Diablo State Park, Walnut Creek. 7.4 miles, 2,152 feet of gain, hard, out and back, 4.7 stars. The highest point for miles, the Sierra crest on a clear day. @castateparks

Panoramic Hill, Chaparral Peak and Strawberry Canyon Loop — Claremont Canyon Regional Preserve, Berkeley. 6.1 miles, 1,505 feet, hard, loop, 4.7 stars. Straight up the Berkeley hills to the full bay.

Wildcat Creek, San Pablo Ridge and Belgum Loop — Wildcat Canyon Regional Park, Richmond. 5.7 miles, 1,305 feet, moderate, loop, 4.6 stars. A ridgeline with bay to Diablo views the whole way.

Springhill, Lafayette Ridge and Briones Crest Loop — Briones Regional Park, Lafayette. 4.2 miles, 1,033 feet, moderate, loop, 4.6 stars. Rolling ranch ridges with Mount Diablo on the horizon.

Dunn, Stream and Graham Loop — Redwood Regional Park, Oakland. 7.5 miles, 1,459 feet, hard, loop, 4.7 stars. The big climb inside the redwoods.

High Ridge Loop — Dry Creek Pioneer Regional Park, Union City. 5.8 miles, 1,227 feet, hard, loop, 4.7 stars. A quieter climb over the south county hills.

Round Top — Sibley Volcanic Preserve, 6800 Skyline Blvd, Oakland. 1.7 miles, 246 feet, easy, loop, 4.6 stars. A volcano summit you reach in two miles, the accessible peak.

Mount Wanda — John Muir NHS, Alhambra Ave, Martinez. 2.4 miles, 544 feet, moderate, out and back, 4.6 stars. Named for John Muir's daughter, oak grassland up to the view.

Nine summits, easy to hard: Mission Peak, Diablo, Panoramic Hill, San Pablo Ridge, Briones Crest, the Redwood Dunn loop, High Ridge, Round Top, and Mount Wanda. Which one is yours?

item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Lakeside Trails

Lake Chabot hides an 8.9-mile shoreline loop that most East Bay walkers never take past the first cove. When the hills go gold and hot in summer, the water trails stay cool. Six East Bay lakeside trails.

Lake Chabot Loop — Lake Chabot Regional Park, Castro Valley. 8.9 miles, 770 feet of gain, 4.8 stars. The full shoreline loop, part paved, with boat rentals at the marina. @ebrpd

Lafayette Reservoir Rim Trail — Lafayette Reservoir Recreation Area, Lafayette. 5 miles, 938 feet of gain, 4.7 stars. A rim loop above the water, with a flat paved lakeside path below.

Lake Anza loop — Tilden Regional Park, Berkeley. About 1.4 miles around the swim lake, sandy beach and summer lifeguards. The one you can actually swim after.

Rocky Ridge and Kings Canyon Loop — EBMUD Lands, Moraga, above Upper San Leandro Reservoir. 6.7 miles, 928 feet of gain, 4.6 stars. Reservoir views the whole ridge, an EBMUD trail permit required.

Jordan Pond via High Ridge — Dry Creek Pioneer Regional Park, Union City. 3.3 miles, 413 feet of gain, 4.7 stars. A pond-and-ridge loop in the south-county hills.

Wildcat Creek Trail to Jewel Lake — Tilden Nature Area, Berkeley. A 1.7-mile flat boardwalk to a little lake, heavy on birds, easy for strollers.

Six for the water: Lake Chabot, Lafayette Reservoir, Lake Anza, Rocky Ridge, Jordan Pond, and Jewel Lake. Which lake gets your summer?

Bay Area Mountain-bike Routes

Tilden alone strings together a 4.3-mile Seaview loop with 994 feet of climb and a straight-shot ridge view, no shuttle and no bridge toll. The East Bay hills are a fire-road playground most riders drive right past. Six East Bay mountain-bike routes.

Seaview and Big Springs Loop — Tilden Regional Park, Berkeley. 4.3 miles, 994 feet of gain, moderate, 4.7 stars. Ridge-top fire road with a bay view. @ebrpd

Wildcat Gorge, Meadows Canyon and Curran Loop — Tilden Regional Park, Berkeley. 3.4 miles, 511 feet of gain, 4.7 stars. A creek-and-meadow loop past Jewel Lake.

Round Top, Volcanic and Skyline Loop — Sibley Volcanic Preserve, Oakland. 3.5 miles, 554 feet of gain, 4.6 stars. Around the extinct volcano and its labyrinths.

West Ridge, Graham and Dunn Loop — Roberts Regional Recreation Area, Oakland. 3.1 miles, 505 feet of gain, 4.7 stars. A tidy redwood-edge loop off Skyline.

Dunn, Graham and West Ridge Loop — Redwood Regional Park, Oakland. 4 miles, 587 feet of gain, 4.7 stars. The Redwood fire-road classic.

Sequoia Bayview Trail — Joaquin Miller Park, Oakland. 4.5 miles, 367 feet of gain, easy, 4.7 stars. A smooth, mostly flat bay-view spin.

Six for the ride: Seaview, Wildcat Gorge, Round Top, the Roberts loop, the Redwood Dunn loop, and Sequoia Bayview. Where do you ride?

item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Dog Trails

There is a 2.5-mile redwood loop in Oakland where dogs run off-leash under the tallest trees around, rated 4.8 stars. Most owners circle the same block; the East Bay hills are built for the long sniff. Six East Bay dog trails.

French, Tres Sendas and Stream Loop — Redwood Regional Park, Oakland. 2.5 miles, 456 feet of gain, off-leash, 4.8 stars. Redwood shade the whole way. @ebrpd

Panoramic Hill and Chaparral Peak Loop — Claremont Canyon Regional Preserve, Berkeley. 6.1 miles, 1,505 feet of gain, off-leash, 4.7 stars. A real climb with a bay payoff, for the athletic dog.

Bay Area Ridge and Round Top Loop — Sibley Volcanic Preserve, Oakland. 3.1 miles, 603 feet of gain, 4.6 stars. Open ridge around the old volcano.

High Ridge Loop — Dry Creek Pioneer Regional Park, Union City. 5.8 miles, 1,227 feet of gain, off-leash, 4.7 stars. Wide-open south-county hills, room to roam.

Springhill, Lafayette Ridge and Briones Crest Loop — Briones Regional Park, Lafayette. 4.2 miles, 1,033 feet of gain, off-leash, 4.6 stars. Cattle-country ridges, keep an eye out for the herd.

Sequoia Bayview Trail — Joaquin Miller Park, Oakland. 4.5 miles, 367 feet of gain, 4.7 stars. An easy shaded out-and-back for the older dog.

Six for the dog: the Redwood French loop, Panoramic Hill, Sibley, High Ridge, Briones Crest, and Sequoia Bayview. Where does your dog run?

item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Backpacking and Overnight Trips

The Ohlone Wilderness Regional Trail runs about 28 miles from Mission Peak through Sunol to Del Valle with backcountry camps you reserve ahead, and most East Bay hikers have no idea they can sleep out this close to home. These are the overnight routes hiding in our own hills. Six East Bay backpacking and overnight trips.

Ohlone Wilderness Regional Trail — Mission Peak Staging, Stanford Ave, Fremont, through Sunol to Del Valle, Livermore. About 28 miles point to point, trail camps by reservation, permit required. The Bay Area's classic multi-day walk. @ebrpd

Rose Peak via Sunol — Sunol Regional Wilderness, 1895 Geary Rd, Sunol. 17.9 miles, 3,927 feet of gain, hard, 4.7 stars. The high country of the Ohlone Wilderness, a long day or a first night out.

Little Yosemite and Backpack Road Loop — Sunol Regional Wilderness, 1895 Geary Rd, Sunol. 5.9 miles, 1,230 feet of gain, moderate, 4.7 stars. Past the Little Yosemite gorge to the Sunol backpack area.

Mission Peak via Ohlone Wilderness Trail — Sunol Regional Wilderness, 1895 Geary Rd, Sunol. 10.2 miles, 2,221 feet of gain, hard, 4.6 stars. The quiet back way up Mission Peak from the Sunol side.

Venados Camp via East Shore Trail — Del Valle Regional Park, 7000 Del Valle Rd, Livermore. 2.4 miles, 144 feet of gain, easy, 4.6 stars. A short walk-in to a lakeside camp, the gentle first backpack.

East Shore and Hetch Hetchy Loop — Del Valle Regional Park, 7000 Del Valle Rd, Livermore. 3.7 miles, 436 feet of gain, moderate, 4.7 stars. Lakeshore miles from the Del Valle base camp.

Six for the overnight: the Ohlone Wilderness Trail, Rose Peak, Little Yosemite, the Mission Peak back way, Venados Camp, and the Del Valle lakeshore. Which one gets your first night under the stars?

item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Birding and Wildlife Trails

Lake Merritt became the first official wildlife refuge in the United States in 1870, right in the middle of downtown Oakland. Pelicans, cormorants, and egrets, no drive required. Eight East Bay spots for birds and wildlife.

Rotary Nature Center at Lake Merritt — 600 Bellevue Ave, Oakland. On the shore of that 1870 refuge, a flat 3.1 mile loop with pelicans, cormorants, and egrets downtown. @ebrpd

Coyote Hills Bayview and Meadowlark Loop — Coyote Hills Regional Park, 8000 Patterson Ranch Rd, Fremont. 4.9 miles, 282 feet, easy, loop, 4.7 stars. Marsh boardwalk, then low hills over the bay.

Arrowhead Marsh — Martin Luther King Jr Regional Shoreline, Swan Way, Oakland. 3.7 miles, 22 feet, easy, out and back, 4.6 stars. Tidal marsh on San Leandro Bay, big on rails and shorebirds.

Cogswell Marsh Loop — Hayward Regional Shoreline, West Winton Ave, Hayward. 6.1 miles, 36 feet, easy, loop, 4.6 stars. A levee loop through restored salt marsh.

Don Edwards SF Bay National Wildlife Refuge — 1 Marshlands Rd, Fremont. The largest urban wildlife refuge in the country, flat salt marsh trails thick with shorebirds.

Vargas Plateau Golden Eagle and Upper Ranch Loop — Vargas Plateau Regional Park, Morrison Canyon Rd, Fremont. 3.9 miles, 518 feet, moderate, loop, 4.7 stars. Open grassland where golden eagles hunt the ridge.

Lake Chabot via East Shore Trail — Lake Chabot Regional Park, 17600 Lake Chabot Rd, Castro Valley. 3.7 miles, 193 feet, easy, out and back, 4.7 stars. A flat stroller friendly shore walk heavy with waterbirds.

Rankin Park to Franklin Ridge Loop — Carquinez Strait Regional Shoreline, Martinez. 4.1 miles, 1,158 feet, moderate, loop, 4.2 stars. A ridge over the strait where raptors ride the thermals.

Eight for the binoculars: Lake Merritt, Coyote Hills, Arrowhead Marsh, Cogswell Marsh, Don Edwards, Vargas Plateau, Lake Chabot, and the Carquinez ridge. Where do you take them?

item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Flat Paved Bay-shore Walks

Point Isabel sits at the Richmond edge of the bay as one of the largest off-leash dog parks in the country, a flat mile and a half of paved shoreline staring straight at the San Francisco skyline. Most people picture hills when they think East Bay trails and skip the water entirely. Six flat, paved bay-shore walks.

Point Isabel Regional Shoreline — Isabel St, Richmond. 1.9 miles, 13 feet of gain, easy, 4.5 stars. Flat bayshore loop, skyline views, and Mudpuppy's dog wash at the gate. @ebrpd

Point Pinole Regional Shoreline — 5551 Giant Hwy, Richmond. 3.2 miles, 147 feet of gain, easy, 4.6 stars, paved. Eucalyptus groves out to a bayside fishing pier.

Crown Memorial State Beach, Shoreline Trail — Otis Dr, Alameda. 4.4 miles, 39 feet of gain, easy, 4.5 stars. The East Bay's swim beach, past the Elsie Roemer bird marsh.

Middle Harbor Shoreline Park — 2777 Middle Harbor Rd, Oakland. 2.5 miles, 29 feet of gain, easy, 4.5 stars. A tidal lagoon with container ships gliding past at eye level.

Bay Bridge Trail — Judge John Sutter Regional Shoreline, Maritime St, Oakland. 5.6 miles, 242 feet of gain, paved, 4.6 stars. A gentle rise out under the new Bay Bridge span to the vista point.

Albany Waterfront Trail — McLaughlin Eastshore State Park, Buchanan St, Albany. 1.9 miles, 68 feet of gain, easy, 4.6 stars, paved. Bay Trail past the Albany Bulb art and the mudflats.

Six flat and paved: Point Isabel, Point Pinole, Crown Beach, Middle Harbor, the Bay Bridge Trail, and the Albany waterfront. Which shoreline gets your Sunday?

item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Paved Rail-trail Rides

The Iron Horse Regional Trail runs almost 28 paved, car free miles down an old Southern Pacific rail line from Concord to Pleasanton, dead flat the whole way, and most East Bay riders only ever see the half mile nearest their house. Our old rail beds became a whole network you can ride for hours. Seven flat, paved East Bay rides.

Iron Horse Regional Trail — Concord to Pleasanton, on the old Southern Pacific line. 27.7 miles, 295 feet, paved, easy, 4.6 stars. Flat, car free, threaded past BART stations most of the way. @ebrpd

Alameda Creek Regional Trail — Niles Canyon, Fremont, to Coyote Hills and the bay. About 12 paved miles one way, 177 feet, easy, 4.7 stars. A straight flat creekside spin to the shoreline.

Bay Trail, Oakland and Alameda estuary — Jack London Square to the Bay Farm bridge. Flat paved bayfront miles with the skyline across the water.

Lafayette-Moraga Regional Trail — Olympic Blvd, Lafayette, to Moraga, on the old Sacramento Northern line. About 7 miles one way, easy, paved, 4.6 stars. Shaded creekside into downtown Moraga.

Contra Costa Canal Trail — Walnut Creek to Concord along the canal. 13.6 miles, 308 feet, easy, paved, 4.5 stars. Flat waterside miles linking parks and BART.

Ohlone Greenway — Berkeley to El Cerrito under the BART tracks. 10.7 miles, 246 feet, easy, paved, 4.4 stars. A flat urban rail trail past murals and community gardens.

Nimitz Way — Inspiration Point, Tilden Regional Park, Berkeley. 3.1 miles, 206 feet, easy, paved, 4.7 stars. The one paved ride with a full bay and Briones view.

Seven for two wheels: the Iron Horse, Alameda Creek, the Bay Trail estuary, Lafayette-Moraga, the Contra Costa Canal, the Ohlone Greenway, and Nimitz Way. Which one do you roll first?

item.content:encoded:
Bay Area National Parks Within a Day's Drive

Pinnacles is the only national park in the Bay Area, an ancient volcano split and dragged some 200 miles north by the San Andreas Fault, and it is one of the last places you can watch wild California condors ride the thermals. Most people drive to Yosemite and never notice the park two hours south. Six national parks within a day's drive of the East Bay.

Pinnacles National Park — 5000 East Entrance Rd, Paicines. Condor Gulch to High Peaks Loop, 5.4 miles, 1,633 feet of gain, hard, 4.8 stars. Wild condors overhead and the rock spires up close. Go at first light in summer, it bakes. @pinnaclesnps

Point Reyes National Seashore — Bear Valley Trailhead, 1 Bear Valley Rd, Point Reyes Station. Bear Valley Trail to the coast, 9.1 miles, 744 feet of gain, moderate, 4.7 stars. A fern canyon that opens onto the open Pacific. @pointreyesnps

Muir Woods National Monument — 1 Muir Woods Rd, Mill Valley. Main Trail, 1.5 miles, 45 feet of gain, easy, 4.8 stars, paved. Old-growth redwoods over 250 feet tall, parking reservation required, book ahead online.

Tennessee Valley Trail — Golden Gate National Recreation Area, Tennessee Valley Rd, Mill Valley. 3.5 miles, 183 feet of gain, easy, 4.7 stars. A flat, stroller-friendly walk out to a hidden pocket beach. @goldengatenps

Mount Wanda — John Muir National Historic Site, 4202 Alhambra Ave, Martinez. 2.4 miles, 544 feet of gain, moderate, 4.6 stars. The oak hills John Muir walked with his daughters, right here in the East Bay. @johnmuirnps

Rosie the Riveter WWII Home Front National Historical Park — 1414 Harbour Way South, Richmond. The Bay Trail runs the waterfront past the historic Ford Assembly Building, free visitor center open daily 10 to 5. The national park in our own backyard. @rosietheriveternps

Six within a day's drive: Pinnacles, Point Reyes, Muir Woods, Tennessee Valley, Mount Wanda, and Rosie the Riveter in Richmond. Which national park do you hit first?

item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Shaded Redwood and Creek Hikes for a Hot Day

The redwoods in Redwood Regional Park once grew so tall that ships in the bay used them as a landmark to steer around Blossom Rock, until they were logged in the 1850s. The second-growth grove that came back is the coolest, shadiest ground in the East Bay. Six shaded redwood and creek hikes for a hot day.

Stream, Mill and French Loop — Redwood Regional Park, 7867 Redwood Rd, Oakland. 4.6 miles, 921 feet of gain, moderate, 4.8 stars. Creekside redwood shade the whole way. @ebrpd

Leona Canyon Trail — Leona Canyon Open Space, Canyon Oaks Dr, Oakland. 2.8 miles, 465 feet of gain, easy, 4.4 stars. A cool creek canyon most Oakland hikers walk right past.

Lower and Upper Huckleberry Loop — Huckleberry Botanic Preserve, Skyline Blvd, Oakland. 2.3 miles, 367 feet of gain, moderate, 4.7 stars. A shaded rare-plant preserve, no dogs on this one.

Wildcat Gorge, Meadows and Curran Loop — Tilden Nature Area, Central Park Dr, Berkeley. 3.4 miles, 511 feet of gain, moderate, 4.7 stars. Creek and bay-tree shade to a little lake.

Pioneer Tree Trail — Samuel P. Taylor State Park, 8000 Sir Francis Drake Blvd, Lagunitas. 2.1 miles, 193 feet of gain, easy, 4.7 stars. An old-growth redwood loop in a cool canyon, worth the drive. @castateparks

West Ridge and Graham Loop — Roberts Regional Recreation Area, 10570 Skyline Blvd, Oakland. 3.1 miles, 505 feet of gain, moderate, 4.7 stars. Redwood shade off Skyline, with a swim pool at the base.

Six for the shade: Redwood Regional, Leona Canyon, Huckleberry, Wildcat Gorge, Samuel P. Taylor, and Roberts. Where do you hide when the hills turn gold and hot?

item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Lakes with a Swim Beach

Shadow Cliffs in Pleasanton was a gravel quarry until the 1960s, and now it is a spring fed swim lagoon with a sandy beach and summer lifeguards. The East Bay hides a handful of lakes you can actually swim in when the valley bakes. Seven East Bay lakes with a swim beach.

Shadow Cliffs — 2500 Stanley Blvd, Pleasanton. A 1.2 mile shoreline loop, easy, 4.4 stars. Spring fed swim lagoon, sandy beach, summer lifeguards and a water slide. @ebrpd

Del Valle — 7000 Del Valle Rd, Livermore. Two swim beaches on a five mile reservoir, lifeguards in summer, with the shoreline trail if you want to walk it off.

Lake Temescal — 6500 Broadway, Oakland. A 1 mile shore loop, 4.5 stars. A sandy swim beach right off Highway 24, summer lifeguards, in town.

Lake Anza — Central Park Dr, Tilden Regional Park, Berkeley. A sandy swim beach tucked in the Berkeley hills with seasonal lifeguards. Check that the beach is open before you drive up.

Don Castro — Woodroe Ave, Hayward. A roped off swim lagoon with a 1.5 mile loop around it, 4.1 stars. Shallow and family friendly.

Cull Canyon — 18627 Cull Canyon Rd, Castro Valley. A small fenced swim lagoon with a sand beach and seasonal EBRPD lifeguards, the quiet one.

Quarry Lakes — 2100 Isherwood Way, Fremont. A swim beach on a Fremont lake with lifeguards in summer, inside a larger recreation area.

Seven to cool off: Shadow Cliffs, Del Valle, Lake Temescal, Lake Anza, Don Castro, Cull Canyon, and Quarry Lakes. Summer algae can close a beach, so call ahead, then which lake gets the towel?

item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Trail-running Loops

Redwood Regional Park hides a shaded single-track called the French Trail, soft dirt under second-growth redwoods that runners loop for the cool and the quiet, 4.6 miles with under a thousand feet of climb. The East Bay hills are laced with runnable loops most people only ever walk. Six East Bay trail-running loops.

Stream, Mill and French Loop — Redwood Regional Park, 7867 Redwood Rd, Oakland. 4.6 miles, 921 feet of gain, moderate, 4.8 stars. The shaded French Trail single-track, soft underfoot. @ebrpd

Seaview Trail — Tilden Regional Park, Berkeley. 6 miles, 1,282 feet of gain, moderate, 4.7 stars. A ridge run with bay-to-Diablo views the whole way.

Rocky Ridge View and Elderberry Loop — Las Trampas Regional Wilderness, Bollinger Canyon Rd, San Ramon. 4.7 miles, 1,112 feet of gain, moderate, 4.7 stars. A quad-burner climb to a wide-open ridge.

item.title: Bay Area Wildlife to See Within a Day's Drive (and When)
item.description: In 1987 there were 22 California condors left alive on Earth. Pinnacles National Park is one of the places that brought them back, and on a clear morning y
item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Wildlife to See Within a Day's Drive (and When)

In 1987 there were 22 California condors left alive on Earth. Pinnacles National Park is one of the places that brought them back, and on a clear morning you can watch a nine-foot wingspan ride the thermals over the High Peaks. The Bay Area is one of the great wildlife corners of California. Six animals to see within a day's drive, and when.

California condors — Pinnacles National Park, Paicines. Look up from the High Peaks or Condor Gulch in the cool morning hours. Year-round, one of the few places on Earth to see a wild condor. @pinnaclesnps

Tule elk — Tomales Point, Point Reyes National Seashore. A free-roaming herd on the northern tip, bugling and clashing antlers in the fall rut from August to October, present year-round. @pointreyesnps

Gray whales — Point Reyes Lighthouse, Point Reyes National Seashore. The migration streams close past the headland from mid-January through April, a prime spot to watch whales from land.

Elephant seals — Chimney Rock, Point Reyes National Seashore. A breeding colony hauls out on the beaches December through March, with pups by January. Winter only, and worth the drive.

Harbor seals and sea lions — Marin Headlands, Golden Gate National Recreation Area. Haul-outs and barking colonies along the coast, with whales offshore in the fall. Year-round. @goldengatenps

Banana slugs — Muir Woods National Monument, Mill Valley. The forest floor's bright yellow icon, out after rain and on cool mornings, while coho salmon spawn in Redwood Creek in winter. Year-round.

Six to see: condors at Pinnacles, tule elk and gray whales at Point Reyes, elephant seals at Chimney Rock, seals in the Marin Headlands, and banana slugs at Muir Woods. Which one first?

Bay Area Free Camping On BLM Land Within a Day of the Bay

Everyone fights for a reserved site at the state park. Within a few hours of the Bay, you can camp free on BLM land for up to fourteen days, no reservation, no fee. Six free BLM camping areas within a day of the Bay.

Knoxville, Berryessa Snow Mountain National Monument — Lake County, about 2 hours. Lower Hunting Creek has no fee and no reservation, serpentine wildflowers in spring and OHV trails all around. @mypubliclands

South Cow Mountain — Near Ukiah, about 3 hours. Free dispersed camping across over ninety miles of off highway and 4x4 trails, the off road weekend.

North Cow Mountain — Near Ukiah, about 3 hours. Free primitive campgrounds at Mayacamas and Goat Rock, twenty six thousand quiet non motorized acres, the opposite of the south unit.

Cache Creek Natural Area — Lake and Colusa counties, about 2.5 hours. Free backpack in camping, California's second largest tule elk herd and bald eagles year round, no cars past the trailhead.

Sacramento River Bend — Near Red Bluff, about 3 hours. Free dispersed camping on miles of Sacramento River frontage, wintering bald eagles and spring wildflowers, hot in summer.

Carrizo Plain National Monument — San Luis Obispo County, about 4.5 hours. Free camping at KCL and Selby plus open dispersed land, the San Andreas Fault and the spring superblooms, go spring or fall not summer heat.

Six free on public land: Knoxville, South and North Cow Mountain, Cache Creek, Sacramento River Bend, and Carrizo Plain. Fourteen day limit, and check the BLM fire order before you strike a match. Which one gets the tent first?

item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Waterfall Hikes Within Driving Distance

Mount Diablo hides a chain of waterfalls that only run for a few weeks after a big rain, and most people who climb the mountain every year have never timed it right. Six Bay Area waterfall hikes worth chasing the storm for.

Mount Diablo Falls via Donner Canyon — Mount Diablo State Park, Clayton. 5.5 miles, moderate, loop, 4.7 stars. A string of cascades that only run a few weeks after heavy rain, the East Bay's best kept wet season secret. Go two days after a storm.

Cataract Falls — Mount Tamalpais Watershed, Marin. 3 miles out and back, hard, 4.8 stars. A staircase of moss lined cascades tumbling down the flank of Mount Tam, loudest and fullest from January to April.

Wildcat Gorge and Cascade — Tilden Regional Park, Berkeley. 3.4 miles, moderate, loop, 4.7 stars. A creekside gorge and a small waterfall a short drive from the flats, gentle enough for kids and dogs on leash.

Dawn Falls — Baltimore Canyon, Larkspur. 2.4 miles, moderate, out and back, 4.7 stars. A slim ribbon dropping through a redwood canyon, the easy one that still feels deep in the woods.

Steep Ravine — Mount Tamalpais State Park, Marin. 4.2 miles out and back, moderate, 4.8 stars. Wooden ladders down a fern canyon, a creek stepping over boulders the whole way toward the sea. The prettiest half day on Tam.

Alamere Falls — Point Reyes National Seashore, Bolinas. About 8 miles round trip from Palomarin, a rare tidefall that pours off a bluff straight onto the sand. Time it with low tide and give the day to it.

Six chasing water: Mount Diablo, Cataract, Wildcat Gorge, Dawn Falls, Steep Ravine, and Alamere. Which one after the next storm?

item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Lighthouses You Can Walk Up to

There is a Victorian lighthouse on a tiny island off Richmond that you can sleep in, reached by the keeper's own boat across San Pablo Bay. Six Northern California lighthouses you can actually walk up to.

East Brother Light Station — Point San Pablo, Richmond. An 1874 Victorian light on an island in the strait, now a five room bed and breakfast reached by the innkeeper's boat. The East Bay's most surprising overnight, book months ahead.

Point Bonita Lighthouse — Marin Headlands, Sausalito. A half mile walk through a hand dug tunnel and across a little suspension bridge to the light on the cliffs, open Sunday and Monday. The Golden Gate framed behind you the whole way.

Point Reyes Lighthouse — Point Reyes National Seashore. Three hundred and eight steps down a wind hammered headland, the best land based gray whale watching in winter. Check that the stairs are open before the drive.

Pigeon Point Light Station — Pescadero. One of the tallest lighthouses on the West Coast at 115 feet, a hostel wrapped around its base and tide pools below. Sunset here is the whole trip.

Point Montara Light — Montara. A working lighthouse that doubles as a bluff top hostel, the cheapest ocean view on the coast and a foghorn for a lullaby. Half an hour past Pacifica.

Point Cabrillo Light — Mendocino. A gentle half mile meadow walk to a restored 1909 light standing over the headlands, whales and wildflowers in spring. Pair it with a Mendocino weekend.

Six lights up close: East Brother, Point Bonita, Point Reyes, Pigeon Point, Point Montara, and Point Cabrillo. Which one for the road trip?

item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Lakes for Kayaking and Paddling

Lake Merritt was the first official wildlife refuge in North America, set aside in 1870, and you can rent a kayak and paddle the middle of Oakland past the herons. Six East Bay lakes to get on the water this summer.

Lake Merritt — Oakland. Kayaks, canoes, and pedal boats from the Lake Merritt Boating Center on a tidal lagoon that has been a bird refuge since 1870. Paddle it at golden hour with the necklace of lights coming on.

Lake Chabot — Castro Valley. The marina at 17936 Lake Chabot Road rents kayaks, pedal boats, and pontoons on a still reservoir ringed by hills. No swimming, but ospreys dive and the coves go quiet fast.

Del Valle — Livermore. A five mile lake south of Livermore with a seasonal kayak and paddleboard center at the east beach, plus swimming and lakeside camping. The launch is calmest early.

Lafayette Reservoir — Lafayette. Rowboats and pedal boats first come first served until four, no private craft allowed, so the water stays glassy under the oaks. The gentlest paddle in the East Bay.

Shadow Cliffs — Pleasanton. An old gravel quarry turned swim lake with boat rentals and a beach, the Tri-Valley's go to when the heat climbs. Paddle in the morning, swim in the afternoon.

Quarry Lakes — Fremont. Kayaking, swimming, and fishing on former quarries along Alameda Creek, flat protected water that is easy for a first timer. A quiet southern option away from the crowds.

Six on the water, Oakland to Fremont: Lake Merritt, Lake Chabot, Del Valle, Lafayette Reservoir, Shadow Cliffs, and Quarry Lakes. Where do you launch?

South Yuba at Bridgeport — South Yuba River State Park, Penn Valley. Long shallow pools and deeper channels under the historic covered bridge, granite slabs to sun on, Kneebone and Family Beach the easy access. The bridge is under restoration but the water stays open.

Hoyt Crossing — South Yuba River, near Nevada City. A quieter local swim about five miles north of town, tiered rocks for gauging your own jump and clear green water below. A short walk keeps the crowds thin.

Yankee Jims — North Fork American River, Colfax. A swimming hole under a one lane bridge deep in gold country, cold pools and a rope of regulars all summer. Go on a weekday and go early.

Johnson's Beach — Russian River, Guerneville. The mellow river town beach, shallow and warm for kids, rentals and shade, the classic lazy float. Rent a canoe and drift the afternoon away.

Healdsburg Memorial Beach — Russian River, Healdsburg. A dammed summer beach with lifeguards, a gentle current, and lawns for the cooler, the family friendly river day. Get there early on a hot weekend.

item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Ancient Redwood Groves Within Driving Distance

The tallest living things on earth grow within a couple hours of Oakland, some of them older than the Roman Empire. Six ancient redwood groves worth a day trip.

Muir Woods — Mill Valley. Cathedral Grove of old growth coast redwoods a half hour from the bridge, a flat boardwalk loop beneath 800 year old giants, hushed on purpose. Reserve parking ahead, it is required.

Big Basin Redwoods — Boulder Creek. California's oldest state park, recovering from the 2020 fire with the ancient giants still standing, the Redwood Loop and Meteor trail reopened. Meteor loop runs 4.8 miles, moderate, 4.7 stars.

Henry Cowell Redwoods — Felton. The Redwood Grove Loop, a flat 0.8 mile stroll among old growth including a hollow giant you can stand inside, easy for every age. Cool and green even in August.

Portola Redwoods — La Honda. A deep quiet park in the Santa Cruz range, the Old Tree trail to a 1200 year old redwood, far enough off the highway to feel genuinely remote. Slate Creek loops for more.

Armstrong Redwoods — Guerneville. The Colonel Armstrong tree at roughly 1400 years old and the Parson Jones tree over 300 feet tall, a flat grove loop and a natural amphitheater. Pair it with the Russian River.

Purisima Creek Redwoods — Half Moon Bay. Second growth redwoods dropping down a coastal canyon toward the sea, fern lined and foggy, a cool climb with an ocean payoff at the top.

Six among the giants: Muir Woods, Big Basin, Henry Cowell, Portola, Armstrong, and Purisima Creek. Which grove first?

Ano Nuevo — Pescadero. The mainland elephant seal rookery, males up to 5000 pounds hauled out on the sand, guided walks in winter breeding season and permit free viewing in the summer molt. Book the winter tour early.

Fitzgerald Marine Reserve — Moss Beach. Harbor seals hauled out on the rocks and one of the best tide pool reefs on the coast at low tide, a short bluff walk to reach it. Check the tide chart first.

Coyote Hills — Fremont. Marsh and bay shoreline in the East Bay, egrets, pelicans, and jackrabbits, boardwalks over the wetland and a hilltop over the whole south bay. The close to home wildlife walk.

Monterey Bay whale watching — Monterey. Summer humpbacks and blue whales feeding on the bay, day boats out of the harbor with near guaranteed sightings from May to November. The deep water spectacle.

item.content:encoded:
Bay Area NorCal Day-trip Beaches

The East Bay is landlocked by the hills, but a short drive over them lands you on some of the best beaches in the state. Six NorCal beaches for a day at the ocean.

Stinson Beach — Marin. A long sandy crescent under Mount Tam an hour from the bridge, lifeguards in summer, a snack shack, and a walkable town. The classic Marin beach day.

Muir Beach — Marin. A small cove at the mouth of Redwood Creek with a driftwood lagoon and the Pelican Inn for a pint after. Quieter than Stinson and made for a picnic.

Rodeo Beach — Marin Headlands, Sausalito. A dark pebbly beach flecked with red and green jasper below the old Fort Cronkhite batteries, dramatic and windswept. Combine it with a headlands hike.

Half Moon Bay State Beach — Half Moon Bay. Four miles of bluff backed sand with a paved coastal trail on top, tide pools at the ends, and pumpkin country behind. Bundle up, it is breezy.

Limantour Beach — Point Reyes. A wide remote strand backed by dunes and an estuary, harbor seals and shorebirds and almost no crowds. Worth the long drive out the peninsula.

Natural Bridges — Santa Cruz. A tide pool cove under a sandstone arch with a monarch butterfly grove behind, family friendly and warmer water than up north. The southern day trip.

Six for the ocean: Stinson, Muir, Rodeo, Half Moon Bay, Limantour, and Natural Bridges. Which coast for your day off?

Bay Area Coastal Bluff and Headland Walks

There is a stretch of old Highway 1 south of Pacifica so prone to collapse that the state finally tunneled around it and handed the clifftop road to walkers. Six coastal bluff walks with the ocean straight down.

Devil's Slide Trail — Pacifica. A paved mile and a half of former coast highway on a sheer cliff, now a car free promenade with whale spouts below and a wartime bunker at the top. Flat and stroller friendly.

Mori Point — Pacifica. A short climb to a grassy headland over the surf, wildflowers and red legged frog ponds below, the ocean on three sides. Sunset here is unreal.

Chimney Rock — Point Reyes. A spring wildflower ridge out to a narrow point, elephant seals on the beach below in winter and gray whales offshore. A mile and a half of pure edge.

Land's End — San Francisco. The Coastal Trail around the city's rocky northwest corner, cypress tunnels, shipwreck views at low tide, and the Sutro Bath ruins. Technically the city, entirely wild.

Fort Funston — San Francisco. A sandy bluff where hang gliders launch off the cliff on the wind and a beloved trail drops to the surf. The most action packed overlook on the coast.

Six on the edge: Devil's Slide, Marin Headlands, Mori Point, Chimney Rock, Land's End, and Fort Funston. Which cliff walk first?

item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Volcanic, Cave and Rock-formation Wonders

Most people do not know there is an extinct volcano in the Oakland hills, its innards tilted up on end so you can walk straight through what used to be underground. Six Bay Area geologic wonders hiding in plain sight.

Sibley Volcanic Preserve — Oakland. The eroded Round Top volcano with a self guided geology trail through tilted lava beds, plus a rock labyrinth in an old quarry pit. Ten million years underfoot.

Vasco Caves — Brentwood. Wind carved sandstone caves and Native American pictographs on a preserve so sensitive you can only enter on a guided reservation trip. Book the naturalist tour ahead.

Pinnacles National Park — Soledad. The spires and talus caves of another ancient volcano, split and dragged up the San Andreas fault, with condors overhead. Bring a headlamp for the caves.

Indian Rock Park — Berkeley. A giant volcanic outcrop rising out of a North Berkeley neighborhood, stone steps to the top and the whole bay at sunset. The city's best free overlook.

Castle Rock — Santa Cruz Mountains. Sandstone tafoni formations pocked like Swiss cheese on a ridge above Saratoga, a favorite of boulderers and kids scrambling the rocks. Cool and forested.

Rock City — Mount Diablo State Park, Clayton. A cluster of sandstone wind caves and honeycombed boulders near the south gate, kids scrambling through the Sentinel Rock tunnels. An easy stop on the drive up Diablo.

Six geologic surprises: Sibley, Vasco Caves, Pinnacles, Indian Rock, Castle Rock, and Rock City. Which one blows your mind?

Big Basin Skyline to the Sea — Saratoga to Santa Cruz. A downhill point to point through the redwoods to the ocean with a camp at Waterman Gap, the classic Bay Area thru hike, reopening as the park recovers. Check current status.

Sunol Backpack Area — Sunol Regional Wilderness. A gentle first backpack, a few miles in to a hillside camp with oak shade and a creek, close enough to bail if the kids melt down. The training trip.

item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Point Reyes National Seashore Hikes

Point Reyes sits on the far side of the San Andreas fault, a peninsula slowly sliding north on the Pacific plate, laced with 150 miles of trail to the sea. Eight Point Reyes hikes for a day on the edge of the continent.

Bear Valley Trail to the Coast — Point Reyes. 9.1 miles, moderate, out and back, 4.7 stars. The gentle valley walk from the visitor center out to Arch Rock and the ocean bluffs. The signature hike.

Tomales Point — Point Reyes. About 9.5 miles out and back through the tule elk reserve at the peninsula's tip, ocean on both sides and bulls bugling in fall. Bring binoculars.

Alamere Falls via Palomarin — Point Reyes. About 13 miles round trip past two lakes to a rare tidefall pouring onto the beach. Time it with low tide and give it the day.

Mount Wittenberg via Sky Trail — Point Reyes. 5.2 miles, moderate, 4.7 stars. A climb to the peninsula's high point through fir forest with ocean views at the top. The lung stretcher.

Sculptured Beach via the Coast Trail — Point Reyes. 6.5 miles, moderate, 4.6 stars. Down to a wave carved beach of sandstone shelves and tide pools at low tide. Check the tide chart.

Chimney Rock — Point Reyes. A short bluff walk out a narrow point, wildflowers in spring, elephant seals below in winter, gray whales offshore. The quick dramatic one.

Estero Trail — Point Reyes. A rolling path along a tidal estuary to Drakes Estero, herons and harbor seals and almost no crowds. The quiet birding walk.

Earthquake Trail — Bear Valley. A flat half mile paved loop straddling the San Andreas fault, a fence offset twenty feet by the 1906 quake. History underfoot, stroller friendly.

Eight on the seashore: Bear Valley, Tomales Point, Alamere Falls, Mount Wittenberg, Sculptured Beach, Chimney Rock, Estero, and the Earthquake Trail. Which first?

More than 400 hidden public staircases and garden paths lace the Berkeley and Oakland hills, most of them known only to the neighbors who climb them. Eight East Bay secret stairways to walk.

Rose Walk — Berkeley. A landmark double stairway designed by Bernard Maybeck in 1913, curving up through a garden between Euclid and Le Roy. The most beautiful stair in the hills.

Tamalpais Path — Berkeley. Stone steps climbing from Euclid up toward the Rock parks, one of the classic north Berkeley path walks. Steep and leafy.

The Cragmont paths — Berkeley. A tangle of steps like Sterling, Acacia, and Easter Way linking the streets around Cragmont Rock Park, a full loop of stairs and views. Bring a map.

Indian Rock and Mortar Rock steps — Berkeley. Stone stairs carved right into the volcanic outcrops, climbing to a sunset view over the bay. The stairs that end at the top of a rock.

The Oakmore steps — Oakland. A network of concrete stairways stitching the Dimond Canyon and Oakmore hills, hidden between the craftsman homes. The Oakland classic.

Crocker Highlands paths — Oakland. Quiet garden stairways winding through one of Oakland's prettiest old neighborhoods above Lakeshore. The genteel stroll.

Rockridge to Claremont paths — Oakland. Hidden lanes and steps linking the streets above College Avenue up toward the Claremont, a leafy climb. The uphill shortcut.

La Loma and Glendale steps — Berkeley. A steep set of hillside stairs with framed bay views between the switchbacks, part of the north Berkeley path grid. The workout with a view.

item.content:encoded:

Angel Island is the largest island in San Francisco Bay, reached only by ferry, with a summit view that takes in the whole bay and a history as the Ellis Island of the West. Eight ways to spend a day on Angel Island.

Mount Livermore Summit — Angel Island. A climb up the North Ridge and Sunset trails to the 788 foot top, a full turn of the bay, bridges, and city. The big payoff.

Immigration Station — Angel Island. The preserved Ellis Island of the West where a quarter million people were processed, the barracks poetry carved in the walls a moving museum. Take the tour.

Ayala Cove — Angel Island. The ferry landing with a visitor center, a green lawn, and picnic tables, the easy base for the day. Start and end here.

Camp Reynolds — Angel Island. A Civil War era army post of brick and white clapboard buildings above a west facing beach. Step into the 1860s.

Battery Ledyard and the missile site — Angel Island. Concrete gun batteries and a Cold War Nike missile radar site, the island's layered military past. Poke through the ruins.

Ferry from Tiburon — Angel Island. The short hop from Tiburon or the longer ride from the city, the approach itself a highlight. Sit up top on the way over.

Angel Island beaches — Angel Island. Quiet coves like Quarry and Perles for a picnic with a downtown skyline backdrop. Pack a lunch.

The Sonoma Coast is where the Russian River pours into the Pacific at Jenner, a wild stretch of bluffs and coves where harbor seals pup on the sand and gray whales pass offshore. Eight Sonoma Coast stops.

Bodega Head — Bodega Bay. A 1.7 mile bluff loop, 4.8 stars, one of the best whale watching perches on the coast in winter. Scan for spouts.

Goat Rock Beach — Jenner. The broad beach at the Russian River mouth where a harbor seal colony hauls out and pups in spring. Keep your distance from the seals.

Kortum Trail — Bodega Bay. A 4 mile bluff path, 4.7 stars, past sea stacks and wildflowers between Shell Beach and Blind Beach. The classic coast walk.

Jenner and the river mouth — Jenner. The tiny town on the hill where the river meets the sea, kayak rentals and a view down the coast. Paddle the estuary.

Salt Point State Park — Jenner. A rugged park of honeycombed tafoni sandstone, tide pools, and a pygmy forest up the hill. Explore the rock formations.

Shell Beach — Bodega Bay. A tide pool cove at the Kortum Trail's south end, rich with anemones and stars at low tide. Time the low tide.

Duncans Landing — Bodega Bay. A dramatic rocky headland and small beach, once a schooner landing, big surf and views. The quick pullout stop.

Fort Ross — Jenner. A restored 1812 Russian fur trading fort on the bluffs, a reconstructed stockade and chapel to walk through. Step into the history.

item.title: Mission Peak and Sunol Hikes
item.description: Eight East Bay hikes around Mission Peak and Sunol, ranked from the lung-buster to the stroll. Fremont and Sunol hold some of the Bay Area's best ridge cli
item.content:encoded:
Mission Peak and Sunol Hikes

Eight East Bay hikes around Mission Peak and Sunol, ranked from the lung-buster to the stroll. Fremont and Sunol hold some of the Bay Area's best ridge climbs, and locals know which trailhead to pick. Here's your map to the good stuff.

Mission Peak via Stanford Avenue — Mission Peak Regional Preserve, Fremont. The classic gut-check: a 3-plus-mile climb to the summit that eats about five hours round trip once you count the photo line at the pole. Only 43 spots in the lot, so it fills before the coffee kicks in. Come on a weekday and you dodge the resident parking rules. @ebrpd

Hidden Valley Trail — Mission Peak Regional Preserve, Fremont. This is the steep line the district itself files under its challenging hikes, the one that turns your calves into a talking point. Open grassland the whole way up and almost no shade, so save it for a cool morning. The reward is that same summit ridge.

Mission Peak via Ohlone College — Mission Peak Regional Preserve, Fremont. The Peak Trail here is the gentler grade and part of the Bay Area Ridge Trail, that 550-plus-mile ring around the bay. Over 900 parking spaces and a four dollar machine, so the walkable payoff is you find a spot without circling. Passes a horse corral and shaded woodland the Stanford side never sees. @ebrpd

Ohlone Wilderness Trail — Mission Peak to Sunol, Alameda County. Twenty-nine miles of ridgeline linking Mission Peak to Del Valle, and here's the 2026 news: as of January 1 you no longer need the old Ohlone permit to hike it. Overnight camping still wants a reservation. Do an out-and-back chunk from the Stanford staging area and turn around when your legs vote.

Flag Hill Trail — Sunol Wilderness Regional Preserve, Sunol. A short 1.26 miles one way, but the switchbacks are steep enough to make it honest work before the view opens on Calaveras Reservoir and the Alameda Creek watershed. Look down and you're standing on fossil-bearing sandstone, an old seabed parked in the hills. @ebrpd

Canyon View Trail — Sunol Wilderness Regional Preserve, Sunol. A gentle 1.39-mile rise through Jacob's Valley that hands you off to Little Yosemite, the scenic long way, not the grind. Weathered serpentine and sandstone outcrops line it, and the oak woodland keeps it civilized. Good pick when the peak crowd wants a mellower local loop.

Little Yosemite (Alameda Creek Overlook) — Sunol Wilderness Regional Preserve, Sunol. A scenic gorge on Alameda Creek about two miles upstream from the Visitor Center, all boulders and green pools. The district officially renamed it Alameda Creek Overlook, and no, you can't swim: endangered species live in that water. Pack a lunch and a flat rock to sit on.

Maguire Peaks Loop — Sunol Wilderness Regional Preserve, Sunol. A 3.9-mile loop off the beaten Sunol track, with views of San Antonio Reservoir and Mt. Diablo and plants that grow rare everywhere else in the park. Park on Welch Creek Road and note the weekend permit fee at the kiosk. Quiet is the whole point out here. @ebrpd

Eight for the Fremont and Sunol high country: Mission Peak from Stanford, Hidden Valley, Mission Peak from Ohlone, the Ohlone Wilderness Trail, Flag Hill, Canyon View, Little Yosemite and Maguire Peaks. Which East Bay climb gets your next cool Saturday?

item.description: Eight East Bay ridge hikes where the Bay Area quietly shows off. Most people gun for Mission Peak and skip the Briones and Las Trampas crests next door, wh
item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Briones and Las Trampas Ridge Hikes

Eight East Bay ridge hikes where the Bay Area quietly shows off. Most people gun for Mission Peak and skip the Briones and Las Trampas crests next door, where 1,483-foot Briones Peak opens a 360 on the Delta, Tam, and Diablo. Contra Costa's best-kept ridges, mapped.

Briones Crest Trail — Briones Regional Park, Lafayette. The spine of the park's 6,256 acres, the ridgeline every other trail climbs to meet. Rolling grassland, big oaks, and grazing cattle that hold the right of way, over a view corridor locals blow past on the drive to Tahoe. @ebrpd

Mott Peak Trail — Briones Regional Park, Lafayette. The 1,424-foot high point most people never bother to name, tucked along the crest between the lagoons and Briones Peak. Short pull, big payoff, and on a weekday the summit is usually yours alone. Bring layers, the wind up here does not negotiate. @ebrpd

Briones Peak — Briones Regional Park, Lafayette. At 1,483 feet this is the park's true summit, and the district's own map promises a 360 on the California Delta, Mount Tamalpais, Mount Diablo, and Las Trampas. Clear winter mornings after rain are the move. Naturalist John Muir, who lived in nearby Martinez, hiked these hills, so you are in good company. @ebrpd

Sindicich Lagoons — Briones Regional Park, Lafayette. Twin ponds sitting right up on the crest, reached off the Lagoon Trail, one of the few flat quiet pockets you will find at this elevation. Bring a snack and take in the whole ridge from a spot most hikers skip while chasing the next summit. Golden hour on the water does the work for you. @ebrpd

Las Trampas Rocky Ridge — Las Trampas Wilderness, San Ramon. A paved service road climbs you toward the 2,024-foot summit, then the wind-sculpted stone outcrops take over, colored by lichen the district calls beautiful. Rocky Ridge View Trail bans bikes, so it stays calm. Give the full ridge and the Devil's Hole area a day if you have one. @ebrpd

Las Trampas Ridge Trail — Las Trampas Wilderness, San Ramon. The east ridge across Bollinger Creek, running toward 1,827-foot Las Trampas Peak, with the district crediting views of the Ygnacio, San Ramon, and Amador valleys plus Mount Diablo and the Carquinez Strait. Reach it via Chamise and the Bollinger Creek Loop. Boots recommended, and that is the park talking. @ebrpd

Eugene O'Neill Site and Bollinger Canyon — Las Trampas Wilderness, Danville. Walk in from Danville up the Iron Horse Trail into Las Trampas and finish at the Tao House, the National Park Service parcel of the Eugene O'Neill National Historic Site. The Park Service runs it by reservation, so call ahead before you count on getting in. Oaks and bay laurel the whole climb, and a canyon that feels a county away from I-680. @ebrpd

Elderberry Trail — Las Trampas Wilderness, San Ramon. A quieter hiker line off the Bollinger Creek valley floor, named for the elderberry that fills the chaparral alongside the manzanita and toyon. A low-key way to warm up a Rocky Ridge day before the grade kicks in. Signed and on the district map, unlike the bootleg paths they ask you to skip. @ebrpd

Eight for the Contra Costa skyline: Briones Crest, Mott Peak, Briones Peak, Sindicich Lagoons, Rocky Ridge, Las Trampas Ridge, the O'Neill canyon walk, and Elderberry. Ridge season in the East Bay runs clear and cool right after the first rains. Which crest do you take first?

item.title: Bay Area Coyote Hills and Fremont Shoreline
item.description: Eight stops on the Fremont shoreline, the East Bay corner most people blow past on the way to somewhere else. Coyote Hills is 1,266 acres of marsh and gras
item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Coyote Hills and Fremont Shoreline

Eight stops on the Fremont shoreline, the East Bay corner most people blow past on the way to somewhere else. Coyote Hills is 1,266 acres of marsh and grassland right on the Bay, dedicated back in 1967, and the Alameda Creek Trail and a 30,000-acre wildlife refuge pick up where it leaves off. This is where the map runs out of pavement.

Bayview Trail — Coyote Hills, Fremont. The paved loop runs 3.5 miles around the hills, flat enough for a stroller and high enough to hand you the whole Bay and the peninsula skyline. Locals know it as Sii 'Imnom 'Ommu in Chochenyo, and yes, the wind up top is part of the deal. Go at golden hour and let the fog do the work.

Red Hill Trail — Coyote Hills, Fremont. A short climb to the top of Red Hill, the high point regulars use to catch the breeze and the long view west over the marsh to the water. The Chochenyo name is Pulteewis Saatos. It is the kind of hilltop that explains why the whole neighborhood grew up facing the Bay. Bring a layer, the wind means it.

Marsh Boardwalk — Coyote Hills, Fremont. A raised walkway carries you out over the cattails and open water without soaking a shoe. That's the point of a marsh you can stand in the middle of. Herons and egrets treat the railings like a front porch. Come early on a weekday and you may have the place to yourself.

Chochenyo trail markers — Coyote Hills, Fremont. In 2022 the park unveiled 35 trail markers carrying names in Chochenyo, the language of the Tuibun Ohlone, whose homeland this is. Bayview reads Sii 'Imnom 'Ommu, Red Hill reads Pulteewis Saatos. Read the signs as you walk and the hills stop being scenery and start being a place with a first name.

Tuibun Ohlone shellmound site — Coyote Hills, Fremont. Tucked in the marsh are shellmounds roughly 2,000 years old, left by the Tuibun Ohlone who have lived with this land since long before anyone drew a property line. You reach them on a naturalist-led tour from the visitor center. That's the respectful way in. Book ahead, the walks fill.

Quarry Staging Area — Coyote Hills, Fremont. A staging area with its own picnic tables, barbecue braziers, water, and shade, first come first served, and a quieter place to start than the visitor center lot. It puts you a short walk from the Bayview loop and the marsh. Pack a lunch and claim a table before noon.

Alameda Creek Regional Trail — Fremont. This one runs 12 miles from the Bay to the mouth of Niles Canyon, and it is two trails in one, an equestrian track on the north levee and a paved bike path on the south, bordering Coyote Hills the whole north edge. Ride it end to end and you cross half of Fremont without touching a street.

Don Edwards SF Bay National Wildlife Refuge — 1 Marshlands Rd, Fremont. The country's first urban wildlife refuge, set up in 1972, 30,000 acres of open bay and marsh with around 280 kinds of birds passing through. Start on the 0.64-mile Tidelands Trail from the visitor center flagpole, over the footbridge across Newark Slough. Trails run sunrise to sunset, so there is no bad time to wander in.

Eight for a Fremont shoreline day: Bayview loop, Red Hill, the Marsh Boardwalk, the Chochenyo markers, the Ohlone shellmounds, Quarry Staging, Alameda Creek, and the Don Edwards refuge. Bike, boots, or binoculars, which way do you point first?

item.description: Eight ways to spend a morning at Rancho San Antonio, the South Bay preserve everyone in Los Altos and Cupertino treats as their backyard. Over 25 miles of
item.content:encoded:
Bay Area Rancho San Antonio, Los Altos

Eight ways to spend a morning at Rancho San Antonio, the South Bay preserve everyone in Los Altos and Cupertino treats as their backyard. Over 25 miles of trail, a working farm, wild turkeys in the meadow, and a lot that fills by 8am on weekends. Dogs stay home here and water taps are scarce, so pack your own. Here is how to do it right, from easy stroll to real climb.

PG and E Trail — The wide gravel road most people start on, flat and easy the first mile out to the farm, friendly for strollers and little kids. Keep going and it drops the gentle act: the full climb runs 3.7 miles and 1,600 feet up to Black Mountain, fully exposed. Walk the easy mile, or commit to the grind and earn the Bay views up top.

Deer Hollow Farm — A 160-year-old working homestead a flat mile in, with pigs, goats, sheep, chickens and a cow, plus the restored Grant Cabin set up like the late 1800s. Free to walk through and a reliable bribe for anyone you dragged along under four feet tall. Open Tuesday to Sunday 8 to 4, Wednesday until 1, closed Mondays.

Rogue Valley Trail — The shaded creek stretch, cool and green when the exposed hills are baking, poppies and lupine along the edges in spring. This is the section the preserve puts on its own postcards, and you will see why. Take it as the mellow way to loop back, or the smart move on a hot afternoon when the ridge turns into an oven.

Wildcat Loop Trail — A three-mile loop, moderate, that follows the creek into a cool fern-walled canyon, climbs through chaparral to open meadows on the ridge, then drops you back at the farm. On a clear day the meadow hands you Mount Tam to the north and Mount Hamilton to the east. The classic Rancho half-day if you run only one loop.

High Meadow Trail — The climb that trades shade for a payoff, up through grassland to a wide-open ridge meadow where the whole South Bay spreads out below you. Moderate, and you feel the elevation in your legs. String it with Upper Wildcat and PG and E for a roughly 6.5-mile loop. Go on a clear winter morning when the air is scrubbed and the views run for miles.

Upper Wildcat Canyon Trail — Push past where the crowds turn around and this becomes the prettiest, quietest part of the preserve, deep canyon and oak woodland with barely a soul on it. Fold it into the full 7.6-mile Wildcat Canyon Loop, moderate, topping out near 1,050 feet with South Bay vistas. This is where Rancho stops feeling like a city park.

Coyote Trail — Down in the county park, an oak-shaded lower route and the one stretch open to horses, so expect the occasional rider. Easy to moderate, good shade, a calmer alternative when the main drag is packed with strollers and trail runners. Keep your eyes up, coyotes and wild turkeys both work this side of the park.

Chamise Trail to the Windmill Pasture — A 2.1-mile gradual climb to a tranquil hidden meadow at the north end, next to Hidden Villa, where a ranch windmill once stood. Bring a sandwich, this is the picnic spot most Rancho regulars never find. Crews cleared a fuel break along Chamise recently, so parts feel open and sunny now. One of the best quiet corners here.

Eight ways through Rancho San Antonio: PG and E Trail for the easy mile, Deer Hollow Farm for the animals, Rogue Valley for shade, Wildcat Loop for the classic, High Meadow for the views, Upper Wildcat Canyon for quiet, Coyote for the oaks, Chamise for the hidden meadow. Check openspace.org before you leave, come early or midday, bring water, leave the dog home. See you out there.
